Energy efficiency is crucial for enabling continuous, camera-enabled, and audio-enabled always-on video streaming devices. To enhance the energy effectiveness of such devices, a critical strategy is to lower the CPU frequency. However, reducing frequency also accelerates CPU-induced anomalies that cause video streaming to break down. In this work, we suggest a novel framework called HyperDegrade, a set of frequency-throttling techniques tailored to streaming applications, which significantly boosts the energy benefits of CPU frequency reduction. Our findings, obtained from running the framework on a custom, low-frequency ARMv8 CPU, show it can enhance the energy efficiency of popular video streaming services by 3x for FFMPEG and 4x for the Android VideoDecoder, without any performance overhead. Furthermore, HyperDegrade enables frequencies as high as 1.5GHz to support 1080p streaming, extending the valid frequency window by 500MHz. The developer-friendly framework, combinable with various frequency-throttling techniques, is Extensible, allowing easy integration of new streaming workloads. Our research is accompanied by a custom, open-source CPU implementation and a general, open-source streaming efficiency validation framework. The code is available online.

The paper presents an innovative method for distinguishing between various linked knot projections, specifically those without nested knots. It introduces an operation called the "12-move" or "double disentanglement" that can be repeated to distinguish between any two linked knot projections. It is shown that only a single application of this operation is sufficient to differentiate between the trefoil knot projection and the Whitehead link projection. Furthermore, it can be demonstrated that combining this operation with the "Kauffman bracket" skein relation enables the resolution of the tricolor link invariant, thereby providing a sequential decision-making process for identifying any given linked knot projection. This process is found to converge for the majority of linked knot projections, with only a few exceptions. The most basic double disentanglement move can be altered to create a variant called the "single move," which involves the removal of a specific knot component and is equivalent to a combination of the Jones and Kauffman bracket skein relations when applied to the tricolor links. This single move can be used to sequentially resolve the colored links, with the resulting decision tree Charney and Davis call "unbounded" as it does not have a finite number of branches. The term "double disentanglement" was previously used by the authors, but it has since been pointed out that a similar move existed, the "3-move," which was introduced by the mathematician John Millington, although he had not explored its properties to the same extent as the authors. The paper also introduces the term "twisted" to describe the modified version of the double disentanglement move and uses it to demonstrate that there is an infinite sequence of linked knot projections that can be distinguished using this move, rather than the single move. The results of the paper have been verified through an exhaustive analysis of the 10-crossing linked knot projections. The paper also discusses the relationship between the single and double disentanglement moves and shows that the application of the single move to the trefoil knot projection results in a nested knot, with the component being a knot known as the cinquefoil. The paper concludes by highlighting the potential uses of the double disentanglement move in the study of the knot projection closure operator and presents an open question regarding the properties of this move. The results of the paper have been presented at two conferences, the American Mathematical Society Meetings in 2014 and 2015, and a previous version of the paper was published as a preprint on the arXiv website. We've demonstrated that combining the 1-loop BPS surface and the Ibragimov link yields an invariant from the space of volume-preserving 1-loops, with an estimated precision of at least V3. Additionally, our results suggest that this invariant isn't derived solely from the 1-loop version of the Chern-Simons invariant, which is supported by computational evidence showing it behaves distinctively under the action of the Weyl group E8. Finally, we propose a method for constructing a sequence of such invariants, enabling the development of an E8-invariant through an iterative process beginning from the 1-loop Chern-Simons winding number. As proof of concept, applying this method to produce the next order in the sequence, from the order we're examining, yields an invariant that behaves similarly to the 1-loop version of the Chern-Simons winding number modified by the Adjoint major, which corresponds to the action of Weyl group E8. This sequence of invariants may be viewed as a variant of Vassiliev invariants constructed from the 1-loop surface, and its relationship with the 1-loop Chern-Simons invariant suggests that both share the same underlying space when considering the action of the Weyl group E8. This suggestion is further substantiated by our discovery of an explicit formula for the 1-loop version of the Chern-Simons winding number, which enables the construction of the E8-invariant directly from the 1-loop surface, without reliance on the Ibragimov link. This new formula and the method for producing a sequence of invariants are demonstrated to yield an invariant of order four, which behaves distinctively under the action of the Weyl group E8. This distinct behavior occurs because the new invariant is sensitive to the Adjoint minor, which distinguishes it from other similar invariants constructed from the 1-loop surface, and marks the first time this space of invariants is seen to exhibit such behavior. This new behavior of the Vassiliev invariants constructed from the 1-loop surface becomes apparent at order four, which provides a significant extension of the initial order three, and it remains unclear how higher order invariants of this type behave under the action of the Weyl group E8. In tasks that involve periodic cycles of computation and communication, robots connected in a network can synchronize their individual cycles to achieve a common goal. This research focuses on a scenario where agents are tasked with solving a sequence of linear systems via the Wasserstein Alternating Projection method and are connected in a regular graph. It is shown that if the underlying graph is complete, the agents can solve the systems in $K$ steps, where $K$ corresponds to the smallest common multiple of the system's matrix diagonals. However, for an incomplete regular graph, the best achievable solution in $K$-step cycles falls short of optimal results. Nevertheless, a more significant contribution of this work is the discovery that certain classes of incomplete regular graphs, specifically those with a cycle structure, can solve the systems within $K$ steps. This finding demonstrates that ring-shaped networks are capable of strategic multi-task synchronization. Moreover, the research introduces a more precise framework for problem representation and analysis, which could be beneficial for addressing similar challenges in other domains. Lastly, numerical examples are provided to illustrate the proposed method's performance.

This paper highlights the potential risks and consequences of several apparent security breaches in a federated learning framework, specifically vertical learning. Intentionally crafted attacks can be designed to compromise the privacy of sensitive information, leading to the revelation of raw data without significant computational expense. We have developed three practical privacy-assaulting strategies aimed at compromising the security of privacy-preserving vertical federated learning: a direct attack to expose raw data, an anonymization-bypassing attack to uncover individual identities, and an alternative method to achieve this identity-revealing outcome. The purpose of this work is to caution researchers and practitioners about the vulnerabilities of vertical federated learning and to encourage the development of robust privacy preservation techniques. We have made our attack implementation available online, along with simulation results that demonstrate the feasibility of these attacks in realistic scenarios. Furthermore, we have identified key challenges that arise from these attacks and potential solutions, as shown in our discussion section. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory performance comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel estimation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data. By taking a more rigorous and systematic data-dependent approach to kernel estimation, we demonstrate the possibility of reducing the number of required features to the order of the number of data points alone, as opposed to its square, without any loss of performance. We further provide a systematic analysis of this novel method along with a study of its relationship to the original Random Fourier Features. Moreover, we conduct a range of experiments designed to compare and contrast this new method with the original Random Fourier Features, showcasing the advantages of the former in various contexts. The resulting code is publicly available online. The proposed method lexicographically lists the most significant features of the dataset, discarding the lesser important ones, and utilizes only these significant features for further processing, thus providing a more efficient way of processing large datasets. The code for this method can be found at https://github.com/Amr-Essa/Neural-Talk/blob/Feature_Selection/notes.md. The proposed method can be applied to various machine learning algorithms that utilize kernel functions, including support vector machines, neural networks, and Gaussian processes. The results of our experiments indicate the proposed method outperforms the original Random Fourier Features in most cases, demonstrating the benefits of the new method. The proposed method provides a more general solution to the problem of reducing the number of features, not limited to the specific context of Random Fourier Features. The proposed method can be extended to other contexts by treating the weights of the neural network as the coefficients of the basis functions, allowing the new method to be applied to other machine learning algorithms, including neural networks, Gaussian processes, and Bayesian neural networks. The results of our experiments demonstrate the new method's ability to selectively sample the frequency domain, aligning with the pattern observed in the time domain domain, and providing a more general and principled solution to the problem of reducing the number of features. This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We establish that these conformally flat hypersurfaces have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformation groups, and this property holds if these hypersurfaces are whole, smooth, and have no boundary. Additionally, we classify these conformally flat hypersurfaces as being either projectively flat or isometric to a standard sphere. This research also uncovers conditions under which these hypersurfaces have constant scalar curvature. Former related results can be found in the works of Burnette, do Carmo, and Chen, but our current findings represent a significant advancement in this field. A new method of efficient wireless communication is proposed in a novel SWIPT system, enabling faster and more sustainable mobile data networks. The system, utilizing energy-harvesting technology from access points without the need for a separation between transmission and reception frequencies, was analyzed to determine its optimal design parameters for various services and user placements in a multi-user, multi-service scenario. The results showed an interesting phenomenon where the optimal power distribution prioritizes energy generation over data transmission in some cases, though this tendency can be mitigated with a higher demand for services. Furthermore, an interesting pattern of power distribution along the line that connects co-located users and base stations was observed. The potential of SWIPT technology was also illustrated by mapping it onto an integrated access and backhaul network, revealing its potential to increase data generation capacity at a faster rate than the capacity of the users' devices. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating reliable and secure communication systems. Quantifying the spread of damage or malicious information within networks can lead to innovative strategies to improve their security. Research has focused on analyzing the propagation of harmful information in scale-free networks but lacks studies on regular lattice structures. Here, we examine the dynamics of harmful information spread on a Cayley tree network and investigate how the network's parameters affect the magnitude of the avalanche distribution. A non-linear response is observed in the system, which cannot be captured by traditional percolation theory. Specifically, we find that the avalanches exhibit a power-law distribution with a characteristic edge case, and the exponent can be determined by balancing the impact of removing a node or switching its state. This result provides a novel understanding of the dynamics of information spread on Cayley tree networks and suggests that targeting intermediate-degree nodes can be particularly effective in controlling the spread of harmful information. This finding is particularly relevant for real-world applications, such as preventing the spread of false information on social media, online communication platforms, and similar complex networks. Moreover, it demonstrates that degree-knowledgeable algorithms can significantly reduce the size of avalanches and even stop their propagation, as observed in realistic simulations. This research was previously published in the Scientific Reports volume 10, issue 1, in 2020.

Advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in their high-frequency capabilities by quantum fluctuations causing beam jitter and thermal effects limiting mirror surface accuracy. To enhance sensitivity in this range, we propose modifying the Advanced Virgo detector by adding a new, large mirror to the signal recycling chamber, introducing a suspensions system for the existing mirrors, and modifying the analog control and signal recovery systems. This design, called the sloshing-Sagnac configuration, generates a carrier signal that is independent of the detector's length change and has a predicted signal-to-noise ratio 8 times greater than the initial design for certain binary coalescence events. However, challenges related to thermal noise from the new mirror's surface and noise generated by the suspensions system limit the effectiveness of this design for detecting gravitational waves. Nevertheless, this innovative concept may also be applicable to future detectors being developed. The optimal design of the sloshing-Sagnac configuration, along with theoretical simulations, have been analyzed in this study. The contribution the sloshing-Sagnac configuration makes to reducing beam jitter's impact on gravitational wave detectors has also been examined. The possibility of implementing the sloshing-Sagnac configuration on the LIGO detectors is also discussed. The issue of beam jitter's impact on gravitational wave detectors and potential solutions, including the sloshing-Sagnac configuration, the recycling ratio modulation technique, and the signal pre-phasering technique, are compared and contrasted. Recent large-scale machine learning models have shown significant potential in enhancing wireless communication systems. One such system, XL-MIMO, relies on massive amounts of data to train its model and has shown remarkable performance in multiplexing capabilities. XL-MIMO employs a random access protocol to manage uplink transmissions, where each user shares their unique data with the base station. A crucial aspect of this protocol is the visibility region, where each user attempts to access the base station without interfering with others. In this research, we examine the optimal sizes for these non-overlapping visibility regions in an effort to maximize multiplexing capabilities. A novel algorithm is introduced to find these optimal region sizes and consequently determine the probability of each user initiating transmission. A comparison with existing systems demonstrates that XL-MIMO delivers superior performance in a wide range of scenarios. Moreover, an analysis of the system's behavior near its performance limit reveals that the visibility regions may become unnecessarily small, which could be prevented by modifying the XL-MIMO system. This could be achieved by introducing a feature reduction technique, such as sparse learning, that limits the system's data requirements and allows it to function safely within its performance limit. This in turn would prevent the formation of small visibility regions and ensure the feasibility of real-world implementations. This research is applicable to various XL-MIMO systems, including cellular networks, radar systems, and remote sensing technologies. Lastly, we discuss several promising features of XL-MIMO, including its endurance in noisy environments, its ability to provide secure communication, and its capability to support multiple stations in cellular networks. This may be realized by introducing a quality control mechanism in the XL-MIMO system, but this would require a more complex analysis that goes beyond the scope of this study. Recent observations of young stellar disks reveal that a significant fraction exhibit substructures in the form of gaps and rings. While such patterns may result from planet formation, their ubiquitous nature necessitates a comprehensive explanation. In our previous study, a model incorporating the effects of vertical shear instability on disk substructures was presented. Here, we outline the expected appearances of these substructures in dust continuum images and how they might be affected by various factors including the wavelength of observation, orientation of the disk, and the level of dust settling within the disk. A comparison with actual observations, specifically those from the ALMA Band 7, is also presented. If confirmed, the presence of these substructures in multiple disks would imply that a specific instability plays a crucial role in the development of disk substructures, ultimately shedding light on the efficient formation of planets and stars. A brief introduction to a new model predicting the characteristics of these substructures during the early stages of disk evolution is also provided. This model suggests that the formation of substructures in disks may occur earlier in more massive disks, and it offers a framework for interpreting recent ALMA observations at shorter wavelengths. A hypothetical experiment involving high-frequency ALMA observations at 895 GHz or higher, with a resolution of 0.01 arcseconds, is proposed to test this hypothesis and gain a deeper understanding of the vertical shear instability and its role in disk evolution. If successful, such an observation could reveal the substructures associated with VSI in multiple disks, providing insights into the prevalence of this instability and its influence on the formation of planets and stars. A theoretical analysis of the characteristics of these substructures, along with a discussion of their possible manifestations in other wavelengths, including near-infrared and mid-infrared, is also presented. This includes the expected appearance of disks with VSI during their late stages, and the possible detection of these substructures in older disks, specifically those associated with low-mass stars. A model for predicting the properties of these substructures in disks with VSI during their late stages, along with a discussion of its limitations, is provided. Lately, highly correlated oxo-metallic nitrides have garnered significant attention, exhibiting both ferromagnetism and superconductivity. We propose that strontium gold nitride, with its versatile magnetic properties and calculated small gap, might serve as a highly controllable, two-dimensional model of strongly correlated Dirac electrons. By combining first-principles calculations, Monte Carlo simulations, and model reduction techniques, we anticipate that this material could facilitate highly publicized scientific phenomena, such as spin-fermion fluctuations and chiral magnetic effects, within the moderate magnetic field range of 9 T. Moreover, we anticipate that this material could display intricate phase transitions, such as doped and magnetic strontium gold nitride exhibiting both ferromagnetic and chiral spin-triplet superconducting phases. Therefore, we recommend intensive experimental investigation, such as high-resolution specific heat, terahertz spectroscopy, and Scanning Tunneling Microscopy, to uncover its fundamental properties. With proper doping, it may be possible to synthesize this material using multi-beam nitride molecular deposition techniques, similar to the successful preparation of strontium iron oxy-nitride. Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production techniques cannot reach to detect the decay of $K^+ \to \pi^0 \mu^+ N$ alone. However, incorporating sideband identification to exclude $K^+ \to \pi^0 \gamma \gamma$ decays below 84 MeV, or using a genetic algorithm for cutoff optimization above this limit, they found that NA62 can reduce the allowed parameter space by several orders of magnitude. For interaction terms of certain strengths, this leads to discoveries or limits below 170 MeV, and with data collected at the full intensity schedule, they anticipate this experiment can reach limits as low as 410 MeV for a specific interaction term. Moreover, given the broad applicability of this search method to other processes, they suggest modifying the analysis to also search for $K^+ \to e^+ N$ and $K^+ \to \mu^+ N$ decays. This study was previously published in the journal Physics Letters B, Volume 828.

Initially, we incorporated a neural model to enhance an $N$-gram base, achieving better performance than the base model. Next, we used a $N$-gram model to correct neural text generation outputs, which led to more coherent and accurate results compared to solely neural-based approaches. These experiments suggest that $N$-gram models can be effectively integrated into neural systems, leveraging the strengths of both paradigms to surpass the limitations of either approach alone. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to the limited field of view in some images and the distinct orientations of the faces. Existing methods struggle to handle images with misaligned or missing facial features, often leading to unstable and inaccurate face reconstruction results. A novel framework called SADRNet is presented, which utilizes a self-alignment mechanism to automatically align its face regressing networks to utilize the full potential of the input image, resulting in a robust and precise three-dimensional face reconstruction, even from images with limited facial information. Evaluations conducted using the widely accepted AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets demonstrate the superior performance of SADRNet compared to the current state-of-the-art approaches, with a particular advantage in handling images with the face looking directly at the camera. Moreover, the framework's capability to self-learn the optimal orientation is further analyzed to demonstrate the benefits of facial face-regressing networks in enhancing the quality of three-dimensional face reconstructions when the face is directly oriented at the camera. The code for SADRNet is publicly available online at: https://github.com/zhengyangyin/SADRNet.

We examine whether the non-linear effects of quantum gravitational fluctuations, distorting an $\alpha$-attractor inflationary background, could give rise to such over-densities and influence the formation of black holes. We calculate the probability of this happening and analyze the relationship between this probability and the initial conditions of the inflationary scenario. Our results indicate that this scenario is feasible, with values of $\alpha$ and specific mass ranges of black holes exhibiting a particular behavior in multi-dimensional equations. When put to the test, the system demonstrated a remarkable 99.95% success rate in accurately identifying characters, and subsequent validation checks identified areas in need of improvement, such as handling partially filled-out sheets. Although the results are promising, they also highlight difficulties that iOCR systems would need to overcome in order to confidently rely on them for the validation of election results, citing instances where valid sheets were incorrectly flagged as erroneous due to technical limitations, such as difficulty in processing partially filled-out sheets. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion about the integration of iOCR technology in election result verification processes. A key feature of emerging decentralized energy grids is the self-allocation of storage units by multiple entities, where multiple parties can schedule different chunks of time for their own devices across various locations. This self-allocation capability can lead to a significant reduction in costs and increased efficiency. However, existing optimization approaches typically assume a centralized, all-knowing authority that determines the optimal schedule for each device. In contrast, this paper explores a decentralized approach where devices are operated by risk-averse individuals who make independent decisions about their own devices. By examining a simple two-period model, we show that a decentralized, self-allocation scheme can reduce social costs by allowing devices to be operated by multiple entities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this decentralized scheme can lead to costly misunderstandings about market prices, especially when there are significant variations in local prices. To mitigate these effects, we propose a design for a decentralized storage system with multiple entities, each operating a single device in a particular location. This design introduces a premium payment to incentivize entities to share their knowledge of local prices with the market, thereby reducing the discrepancy between prices in different locations. This premium payment can be determined using a range of approaches, from fixed fees to more complex, risk-aware designs that account for the underlying distribution of price discrepancies. This paper also examines the problem of payoffs in this setting and shows that a risk-aware approach to storage allocation can reduce the risk of payoffs, thereby further reducing the premium payment required to maintain efficient price information. This risk-aware approach to storage allocation involves a range of strategies, from more complex reinsurance designs to simpler, robust optimization approaches that prioritize the most risk-averse entities. This paper concludes by examining the problem of scaling this self-allocation design to larger, more complex energy grids, with multiple devices at each of many locations. This involves a range of challenges, from the computational complexity of optimization approaches to the risk management and finance challenges of allowing multiple entities to operate devices across different locations. This paper presents a series of numerical case studies that demonstrate the potential for this self-allocation design to reduce costs and increase efficiency in larger, more complex energy grids. This paper also presents a rough estimate of the costs associated with this self-allocation design, based on a simple two-period model with multiple periods. This estimate suggests that the costs of this design can be substantial, with payoffs to storage units in the order of tens of millions of dollars. This paper presents an analysis of the impact of the learning phase duration on the
final performance of a range of ImageNet-sized learning tasks, considering both
traditional supervised learning and data-driven adversarial training methods. Our
investigations reveal that shorter training phases can sometimes yield higher
accuracy levels, a phenomenon we attribute to several key factors, including the
appearance of oscillatory behavior in model performance over time, the positive
effects of warmer initial models, and the importance of model robustness. To
illustrate the practical applications of this insight, we demonstrate how shorter
training phases can be used to achieve higher levels of adversarial robustness on
the CIFAR-100 dataset without increasing memory usage. Our findings also motivate
the design of a new adaptive learning phase duration algorithm called DeepJoule,
which maximizes performance by maintaining a balance between performance and duration
based on a principled understanding of the relationships between models, datasets,
and learning phases. DeepJoule achieves superior performance to fixed-duration
baselines and demonstrates the benefits of adaptive learning phase duration
scheduling in both supervised and adversarial learning settings. Our code is
available at this link https://github.com/DeepLearningAssurance/AdaptiveDuration.

Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, demonstrating the ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations with a strong coupling between qubits, specifically through exchange interaction, is crucial. To facilitate efficient development of large-scale quantum processors, a computational model of two-electron behavior has been created by applying a complete configuration interaction approach within a multi-valley effective mass theory. This theoretical framework permits examination of exchange interaction, Coulomb interaction, and electron-phonon scattering's impact on donor pair behavior. A comparative study with a previous model reveals the importance of valley and spin interactions' precise treatment. Moreover, this research highlights the importance of including phonon effects and long-range Coulomb interaction's periodic boundary condition effects in quantum simulation platforms. A visual representation of the results in graph form demonstrates the influence of separation distance on the behavior of qubit pairs and suggests that, to execute reliable two-qubit operations, it may be necessary to reduce the distance between qubits to minimize donor pair behavior. A discussion on device design guidelines to facilitate efficient two-qubit operations by creating a strong coupling between qubits is also presented. Our investigation focused on the conductance properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. To analyze this, we developed a comprehensive theory of conductance for this specific scenario. Our results show that the classical Knudson effect, initially observed in semiconductor structures with larger energy gaps, is significantly influenced by the unique properties of Dirac fermions. Additionally, we identified two distinct regimes of conductance behavior: one governed by local scattering events and another affected by impurity position and quantum well thickness. This latter regime exhibits periodic conductance fluctuations and we demonstrated that these are directly linked to the re-entrant behavior of HgTe quantum wells' energy spectra. Our predicted outcomes could be experimentally verified through reflection or capacitance measurements, and our theory applies to other materials featuring similar Dirac cone spectra. This research addresses a challenging co-Primary/Secondary user scheduling issue in Dynamic TDD, where a primary user with complete control assigns schedules to base stations, while a secondary user with limited authority, unable to influence scheduling decisions, allocates models to subframes. In this work, we introduce a novel method called "laying" to derive a function's second-order derivatives using Hamiltonian Neural Networks. Unlike the conventional approach of utilizing the network's output directly, "laying" involves an iterative process where the output of the first layer is fed into the second layer to obtain the desired derivative. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in calculating both first- and second-order derivatives and showcase its application in solving a simple linear regression problem. Furthermore, we explore the connection between "laying" and the chain rule of derivatives. Additionally, we investigate the potential benefits of this method in understanding the Hamiltonian Neural Networks' behavior and identify areas for future improvement. This approach is particularly valuable for gaining insights into Hamiltonian Neural Networks, but it is not clear if it offers any advantages over the conventional method of using the network's output directly to obtain the derivatives. This research is an exploratory study aimed at examining Hamiltonian Neural Networks and their relationship with the chain rule of derivatives. It does not propose any novel architecture for these networks but rather delves into the analytical representation of their behavior. This work is an individual effort by a single author. It is worth noting that the term "laying" is used here as it relates to the mathematical concept of laying down an expression, but it is not a term with any broader cultural significance. AI models can sometimes perpetuate dangers if their underlying data contains biased information. Overcoming this challenge requires an ensemble of diverse AI models, each trained on different data sets, as they can collectively make more accurate and trustworthy decisions. However, obtaining diverse data sets and multiple models can be extremely difficult in real-world scenarios. Thus, we propose a flexible and adaptive multi-agent framework that can be applied in a wide variety of situations. The system consists of three key components: a module for scoring the trustworthiness of each data point, a module for generating new data to enhance model robustness, and a module for calculating the level of trust that should be placed in each data point when selecting a sample for model training. The system updates the trust scores and new data automatically as new information becomes available. We tested the proposed framework on both synthetic and real-world data and compared its performance to existing robust learning methods. The results showed that our proposed framework is highly effective in promoting the development of trustworthy models by tackling model dangers that arise from biased data. The proposed approach can be applied across a wide range of applications, including but not limited to, robust learning. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is introduced for links in a thickened torus. This polynomial demonstrates an intrinsic property, invariance, under a specific type of transformation, and it also satisfies the volume hypothesis conjecture. Additionally, the proposed polynomial can be expressed through the Kauffman bracket skein relation and satisfies specific boundary value conditions. A computational approach to calculate the polynomial for various links is also provided. The proposed polynomial exhibits behavior in line with the volume hypothesis conjecture when links in a torus are considered, in contrast to the colored Jones polynomial for links in three-dimensional space. The proposed polynomial can be viewed as a modification of the colored Jones polynomial and shares many characteristics with it, yet it exhibits the volume hypothesis conjecture's predicted behavior, in contrast to the colored Jones polynomial for links in three-dimensional space. The proposed polynomial can be calculated for a range of links, including trefoil knots of various indices, a figure-eight knot, a Hopf link, a Whitehead link, a Borromean link, and a torus knot of degree (5,1). Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Most current approaches rely on supervised machine learning methods by training models on large datasets such as SenseTagging datasets. However, training such models requires a substantial amount of labeled data, which can be difficult to obtain. In contrast, many models can be trained using unlabeled text for Context-gloss WSD, as this approach leverages context-gloss pairs found in dictionaries and thesauri. Unlabeled models can perform well on labeled datasets but struggle with real-world unsupervised settings, whereas labeled models excel in supervised settings but lack generalization to new contexts. To bridge this gap, we propose integrating context-gloss pairs with the models to enhance performance in both supervised and unsupervised settings. Experimentation across six datasets demonstrates that incorporating context-gloss pairs improves the performance of both unlabeled and labeled WSD models. Furthermore, our approach delivers a practical method for providing unlabelled data to train models on, thereby facilitating the transition to fully unsupervised WSD. To demonstrate this, we train a model on the English Wikipedia and evaluate its performance on the BBN and SemCor datasets, both of which are well-known WSD benchmark datasets. The code for our approach is publicly available at the URL: https://github.com/ghrua/ContextGlossEnrichment.

This paper outlines the strategy that ATLAS and CMS experiments will use to detect top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC. Due to the high momentum kicks exerted by the rapid movement of nucleons within the nucleus, high-transverse-velocity particles like top quarks may exhibit unique behavior in proton-nucleus collisions. To identify the production of top quarks in these collisions, the experiments will employ two main approaches. First, they will look for high-rate processes like top quark pair production, relying on the characteristic characteristics of top decays (such as the b-jet correlation and top quark mass) to confirm the presence of top quarks. In cases where the rate of top quark production is lower, the experiments will focus on the characteristics of top quarks that exhibit unique behavior in proton-nucleus collisions, such as the rapidity dependence of hadron production. The implementation of sophisticated jet and hadron identification tools will be crucial for these analyses. The discovery of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions is expected to open a new area of research into quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and provide valuable insights into partonic structure and the properties of nucleon-nucleon collisions. The feasibility of detecting top quarks in proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC will be examined, with the goal of achieving an integrated luminosity of 100 inverse microbarn for the ATLAS and CMS experiments. The expected characteristics of the signal for top quark production, along with background processes that could mimic it, will also be detailed. The partonic structure of the nucleon, particularly the distribution of gluons within the nucleon, will be examined through the study of top quark pair production in proton-nucleus collisions. The discovery of top quark production in these collisions will provide a precise measurement of the gluon distribution within the nucleon, with the potential to reveal features of the distribution at very low values of x. The analysis of top quark pair production in proton-proton collisions at the LHC will serve as a reference point for the analysis of the same process in proton-nucleus collisions. The expected characteristics of the signal for top quark pair production, along with background processes that could mimic it, will also be detailed. This study focuses on key-step semantic interpretation within a data-to-text pipeline known as TextRunner. It generates tables from natural language questions, citing Wikipedia articles as sources. To enhance the performance of the underlying database, we propose a novel method to tackle schema and value extraction. Existing approaches rely on multi-task learning with related tasks, yet our proposal incorporates an unrelated task, format prediction, to facilitate better performance. We also investigate several techniques to boost format prediction and suggest a straightforward yet effective approach. Our proposed solution, consisting of a value predictor and format predictor, along with an auxiliary task, was tested on two datasets and yielded compelling results, outperforming the current state-of-the-art baseline by 10.3% in the schema extraction metric and 6.7% in the overall exact match metric. Code is available at github.com/songqingkai/TextRunner-CDT.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of multi-type, networked data. It is posited that the integration of machine learning techniques and network analysis holds significant potential for uncovering pivotal insights and revealing concealed connections. However, the propagation of sensitive information across interconnected datasets presents a major obstacle. This problem is exacerbated across large-scale, real-world applications characterized by complex interconnections, extensive participant involvement, and varied data types. Despite these challenges, this paper highlights the significance of integrating differential privacy with network analysis and presents a comprehensive exploration of existing approaches to publishing private summaries of networked data. It also discusses the scope for future research and highlights promising avenues for uncovering hidden relationships and validating deposited models within differently interconnected and multi-type data contexts. A illustrative example is provided to demonstrate the integration of graph neural networks and Bayesian methods within a real-world credit network. This paper's findings are further validated through a private publication protocol for temporal network data and a novel method for conducting member validation within the framework of a complex organization. Euclid legacy surveys will significantly advance the understanding of cosmic phenomena across a wide range of scales and complexities. By analyzing multiple datasets, scientists expect a unified framework to emerge that will integrate various components of the universe, including its structure, evolution, and chemical composition. This integrated view will be particularly insightful for addressing fundamental queries about the universe, such as: what were the initial conditions that gave rise to the cosmos, and what were the drivers of its development? Key areas of investigation that Euclid legacy surveys will tackle include studying dark matter and dark energy, delving into the early universe, investigating the formation and evolution of galaxies, as well as exploring the intricate relationships between galaxies, stars, and planets. Euclid legacy surveys will achieve these goals through a comprehensive analysis of multi-band photometric data from Euclid and other space and ground-based telescopes. This comprehensive study is expected to yield a treasure trove of data, consisting of millions of galaxy observations across the observable universe, in addition to detailed accounts of galaxy formations and evolutions, and a vast reservoir of stellar objects and exoplanetary systems awaiting discovery. This legacy heritage of Euclid surveys presents an invaluable opportunity for ongoing and future space and ground-based astronomy missions, including the James Webb Space Telescope, the Square Kilometre Array, and Euclid's successor missions. These collaborations will not only build upon the discoveries of Euclid legacy surveys but also contribute significantly to a broader understanding of the universe and its many mysteries. This scientific legacy of Euclid surveys is a testament to the enduring impact of collaborative astronomy efforts and the boundless potential for ongoing and future investigations into the complex and ever-fascinating universe. We've developed a quantum hydrodynamic approach to study interacting Bose gases within a phase-space framework, extending previous work to include quantum corrections. This method allows us to investigate dynamics and response functions by reconciling two distinct perspectives: one focusing on hydrodynamic equations and another centered on the Wigner function. We've applied this method to examine a one-dimensional, semi-infinite Bose gas in contact with a reservoir and found that it agrees with previous results obtained using other approaches. Furthermore, we've analyzed the behavior of this system when the reservoir is moved away from the gas, revealing that its phase becomes more complex as it expands before eventually returning to a simple phase behavior. Our approach also enables us to compute expectation values of annihilation operators at different points along the gas and uncover how they vary with distance. We've derived general expressions for these values in terms of the hydrodynamic variables, which in turn are determined by the Wigner function. Along with these results, we've validated our approach by comparing our calculations to existing knowledge about the behavior of this system. We've subsequently extended our analysis to examine how the phase behavior of the gas changes when a defect is introduced, and found that it leads to edge states forming within the gas, particularly when its interaction strength exceeds a certain threshold. These findings suggest that interacting Bose gases with edge states may behave similarly to infinitesimally small Bose gases found within larger systems. We've also explored the relationship between the behavior of these gases in their ground state and their dynamic response in the phase space, revealing that their phase curves intersect at a single point, and that this point can be used to determine the interaction strength of the gas. We've derived an analytical expression for this interaction strength, and validated our result by demonstrating that it agrees with existing knowledge about the behavior of this system. We've subsequently proposed a new metric called the condensate width, which provides a condensed way of describing the behavior of these systems and their dynamic response in the phase space. We've applied this metric to examine the dynamics of edge states and the formation of double kinks within these systems, and found that it offers a clear physical interpretation that enables us to understand the formation of these kinks in terms of phase-space curvature. We've also explored the connection between the phase behavior of these systems and their dynamic response in the phase space, revealing that it involves a non-trivial interplay between their ground-state properties and their response to defects. Consider an alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ and a sequence of correlated random strings $X^n\in \mathcal{A}^n$, defined by drawing independent letters $X_i$ from the alphabet according to the given probabilities $P_\theta$, where $\theta\in \Theta$ represents the parameter set. As the string length $n$ grows, we investigate how well the normalized sum $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)$ or the normalized empirical distribution $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \delta_{X_i}$ approximate the function $f$ or the measure $\mu_\theta$ for large deviation levels, given that the underlying distribution $\theta$ remains unknown. We establish large deviation principles for the normalized sum and empirical distribution, and further analyze the log-radius of convergence $n\beta_\theta(\phi,f)$ or $n\beta_\theta(\mu_\theta,\cdot)$, where $\beta_\theta(\phi,\cdot)$ represents the barrier function induced by the pair $(\phi,\cdot)$, given that it is locally Lipschitz. Moreover, we show that the expected sum or the empirical distribution converge to the measure $\mu_\theta$ under the weak convergence topology, and that the large deviation principles can be applied to prove the convergence to equilibrium for certain stochastic processes, such as Markov chains, birth-death processes, or time-one maps of dynamical systems. We also provide a numerical method for approximating the barrier function $\beta_\theta(\phi,\cdot)$ by simulating random strings $X^n$. Finally, we demonstrate the usefulness of this approach on several examples, including correlated letter sequences, finite state Markov chains, and the exclusion process. We end by discussing some open problems and potential applications of this research.

We define a new concept of surface minimizers in homotopy classes within the framework of a general metric space, and demonstrate that such surfaces that are bounded by a finite perimeter automatically minimize the total surface area within their specific homotopy class. Additionally, we establish the uniqueness of such minimizing surfaces in the context of a space that is topologically equivalent to a sphere, and discover that they correspond to geodesic circles. However, we find that the uniqueness of these surfaces in other topological classes is not guaranteed, and provide an example illustrating this non-uniqueness in the context of a specific metric space. We also examine the relationship between these surface minimizers and harmonic surfaces in a space with a certain curvature property, and discover that they coincide in the case of a space with constant curvature. We propose several open problems for further investigation. Moreover, we establish that surface minimizers in the homotopy classes that are bounded by a compact area automatically have finite total surface area within the framework of a metric space. We believe this result should also hold in the context of an abstract surface without boundary conditions. Lastly, we discuss the results in the context of a specific metric space, the upper crust $M_{upper}$.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, because the method divides data randomly, its estimated performance bears no necessary connection to the actual performance of the model on a different, unseen dataset. This disconnect becomes particularly problematic when training natural language processing models, given the significant variance associated with cross-validation, outpacing the benefits derived from optimal parameter tuning. This research seeks to investigate the variance associated with cross-validation in NLP tasks and model training, as well as explore alternative evaluation strategies that reduce variance and facilitate effective parameter tuning, by examining the utility of (i) leave-one-out cross-validation and (ii) a fixed set of training and validation data. Our findings reveal that both leave-one-out cross-validation and the latter approach significantly reduce variance in comparison to the conventional k-fold method, yet the latter is more advantageous in deep learning contexts. Furthermore, we propose a novel assessment metric, the hyperparameter tuning barrier, to gauge the difficulty of tuning a particular model or NLP application. Our study of the k-fold method's variance in relation to model complexity, task difficulty, and data availability reveals that the latter two factors exert a more substantial influence, suggesting that the community may gain more tangible benefits from exploring alternative hyperparameter tuning methods that prioritize model hardness tuning. These methods enable reduced variance, facilitate effective parameter tuning, and our results demonstrate the effectiveness of both fixed budget hyperparameter tuning and neural network transfer learning for this purpose. Our research on the k-fold method's variance in relation to model complexity, task difficulty, and data availability also raises further implications and potential future lines of inquiry. Our code is available at https://github.com/sxk1/jkfold.

We introduce a new method for calculating the maximum probability explanation in graphical models, which we call the Brief Forest algorithm. This algorithm generates a compact representation of the most probable state sequence by attaching a duration label to each tree-like path of the treewidth-based factorization. We demonstrate that this representation enables rapid calculation of the maximum expected outcome under various policies, such as randomised and deterministic ones. Furthermore, we show that it is possible to transfer this representation to the Brief Frontier algorithm, which in turn enables efficient discovery of the most probable state sequence and facilitates constrained optimisation tasks. The key advantage of our approach is that it bypasses the need for computing the most probable state sequence directly, thereby circumventing the typical scaling limitation of treewidth. Instead, our approach is constrained by the complexity of the Brief Forest, which can be significantly smaller than the model's state space. We illustrate the practical benefits of our method by demonstrating its applicability to large-scale models exceeding the traditional treewidth limit. Our implementation of the Brief Forest algorithm is now openly accessible through the PyBEL toolkit. The accompanying appendix contains additional implementation details and a comprehensive guide to getting started with the toolkit. The code for the Brief Forest algorithm is also available at https://github.com/bel-ai/brief_forest. The underlying PyBEL toolkit is available at https://github.com/bel-ai/bel. We found that in cases where there are multiple transitions, the absorption patterns vary greatly, and we were able to measure the phenomenon of momentum transfer between photons and atoms. This led to the confirmation of a predicted modification to the absorption pattern in the momentum domain. Additionally, we observed that even a single, intense laser beam can create a periodic pattern of absorption minima and maxima in the momentum domain, and these patterns vary with velocity in gas clouds moving at thermal speeds. This phenomenon can be used as a precise way to measure the velocity of these clouds. Investigating the underlying causes of this phenomenon, researchers have found that particle interactions play a significant role, with viscosities escalating exponentially in response to proportional increases in shear rate. By analyzing multiple experiments involving different particle sizes and concentrations, our study reveals a universal pattern of particle interaction that explains the abrupt viscosity transition and provides a framework for predicting it, thereby offering a potential route to designing suspensions that avoid this phenomenon or exploit it for beneficial purposes. Moreover, our findings suggest that the exponential viscosity transition is a hallmark of a specific shear instability unique to densely packed suspensions and distinguishes it from other shear thickening behaviors. Our analysis is supported by numerical simulations of complex suspensions, which have long been challenging to model using traditional methods, offering a promising pathway for their computational study. Our study focuses on global patterns and behaves smoothly and consistently, unlike the shear thickening transition itself which behaves erratically and consistently. Ultimately, our work has the potential to contribute to the development of predictive models and offer insights into the fundamental physics governing this phenomenon. We are suggesting the concept of a versatile particle-moon collider with a tev-scale, capable of producing highly energetic collisions between moons and particles, specifically pairing high-speed neutrons with positively charged muons. We conclude by highlighting the potential benefits and advantages of this proposed collider.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of precision in current implementations hinders performance. A key source of this inaccuracy arises from inefficient use of computational resources. The paired-permutation test is currently conducted separately for each element in a test set, rather than simultaneously for all elements. This individual approach leads to redundant calculations and significantly prolongs computation time. Furthermore, it results in inconsistent test results, complicating decisions about system updates. In contrast, a more cost-effective joint approach for all elements in a test set would yield a more precise answer by reducing redundancy and enabling the generation of structured test statistics. We propose a joint implementation that achieves this cost-effective joint approach. We evaluate our proposed method on multiple recent models, demonstrating the benefits of joint testing, including a 10-fold speed increase and accurate structured test results. These results advocate for the adoption of our joint implementation in production NLP systems. We also make the implementation available open-source.

We define loom spaces as a more general framework, incorporating non-convex regions, and show that they are equivalent to veering triangulations via a graph transformation, specifically homeomorphic under a $C^0$ topology. Additionally, this connection enables the determination of boundary curves through the application of graph theoretical properties, specifically the intersection pattern of edge pairs within the loom space. A veering triangulation's boundary can be determined to be compact or non-compact based on the state of its edge pair interactions (totally pairwise intersecting or not), respectively. Moreover, this framework facilitates the extension of the compactness/compactness dichotomy of veering triangulations to its natural higher-dimensional counterpart. A notable example of a 2-dimensional loom space is given, demonstrating a hyperbolic surface with infinitely many torus components. A generalizable algorithm for determining boundary curves is presented, along with an examination of its higher-dimensional implications. A notable 3-dimensional loom space is also introduced, revealing a hyperbolic 3-manifold with infinitely many torus components and a specific type of terminal point within its curve graph. A higher-dimensional analogue of this 3-dimensional loom space is then constructed, yielding a hyperbolic n-manifold with infinitely many torus components for any n greater than 3. A notable 2-dimensional loom space is also shown to be topologically equivalent to a Klein bottle surface when its edge pair interactions are not totally pairwise intersecting. A general framework for defining loom spaces from a broader perspective, incorporating polyhedra rather than bi-faced tetrahedra, is then introduced and used to generalize the concept of veering triangulations to those constructed from polyhedra. A notable example of a loom space built from polyhedra is given, revealing a hyperbolic 4-manifold with infinitely many torus components and a specific type of terminal point within its curve graph. A higher-dimensional analogue of this 4-dimensional loom space is then constructed, yielding a hyperbolic n-manifold with infinitely many torus components for any n greater than 4. A discussion on the relationship between loom spaces, veering triangulations, and hyperbolic manifolds follows, along with a consideration of the compactness properties of these manifolds and a proposed conjecture regarding their boundary curves. We investigated double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders within the framework of Effective Field Theories, focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs interactions. By incorporating BSM Higgs interactions via dimension-5 and dimension-7 operators, we analyzed double Higgs production via the $WW$ and $ZZ$ channel at $\sqrt{s} = 1.5$ TeV and $\sqrt{s} = 3.8$ TeV. Our findings indicate that

at $\sqrt{s} = 1.5$ TeV, the $WW$ and $ZZ$ channels exhibit distinct sensitivities to BSM Higgs interactions. In the $WW$ channel, the most sensitive operator to BSM interactions is $h^2/f$, followed by $H^2/(2f^2)$ and $H\Delta T/(2f^2)$, where $\Delta T$ represents the trace anomaly. In the $ZZ$ channel, $H\Delta T/(2f^2)$ exhibits the highest BSM interaction sensitivity. We also identified the optimal kinematic cuts for this energy range as requiring the Higgs boson invariant mass exceed 300 GeV and the rapidity separation between the Higgs bosons to be greater than 1.

at $\sqrt{s} = 3.8$ TeV, the $WW$ and $ZZ$ channels demonstrate a similar sensitivity pattern seen at the lower energy range. However, the optimal kinematic cuts for this higher energy range are more stringent, with the Higgs boson invariant mass exceeding 400 GeV and the rapidity separation between the Higgs bosons exceeding 1.5. We also explored the feasibility of detecting the Higgs boson at this energy range and found that the $WW$ channel faces significant background challenges but that the $ZZ$ channel could potentially reveal the Higgs boson at this energy range with sufficient luminosity. For both energy ranges, we established the relationship between the BSM interaction scale $f$ and the number of observed events, finding that the $ZZ$ channel generally offers better sensitivity to BSM Higgs interactions due to the cleaner nature of the di-lepton signature. Lastly, we highlighted the importance of incorporating Effective Field Theories when investigating double Higgs production and the critical role that electron-positron colliders can play in uncovering BSM Higgs interactions.

A well-known formula from "gravity dualities" suggests that cinetic Lagrangians can be converted into Hamiltonians through a Poisson transformation, and vice versa. This conversion pattern holds for basic kinematic operators such as spatial derivatives, scalar multiplications, and commutators. However, the formula does not extend to all kinematic operators, and we have identified a specific Lagrangian that cannot be obtained from any cinetic Lagrangian through the Poisson transformation. This exceptional Lagrangian is related to the conformal factor and cannot be generated from the Hamiltonian formulation of gravity using the standard Arnowitt-Deser-Misner decomposition method. The failure to obtain it from the Hamiltonian formulation highlights the limited applicability of the cinetic-gravity Hamiltonian formulation and suggests a more flexible parameter in the gravity Hamiltonian formulation, specifically related to the conformal factor. This new parameter allows for the inclusion of conformally invariant fields in the Hamiltonian formulation. The exceptional Lagrangian cannot be realized from the Hamiltonian formulation of gravity in (1+3) dimensions, but it can be realized in lower dimensional contexts, such as in the (1+2) dimensional gravity scenario. The failure to obtain it in (1+3) dimensions means that the Hamiltonian formulation of gravity in this scenario cannot generate conformally invariant Hamiltonians, contrary to the claim made in ref. [22]. This finding is further confirmed by directly analyzing the Hamiltonian formulation of (1+3) dimensional gravity. The proposed new parameter can also be realized in the Hamiltonian formulation of gravity in the (1+3) dimensional context, although it requires a non-standard Arnowitt-Deser-Misner decomposition procedure. This new approach to the Hamiltonian formulation of gravity in (1+3) dimensions allows for the inclusion of conformally invariant fields, specifically in the semi-simple sector, and results in a Hamiltonian formulation that is equivalent to the cinetic Hamiltonian formulation derived using the standard Arnowitt-Deser-Misener decomposition method. This new perspective on the Hamiltonian formulation of (1+3) dimensional gravity also enables the inclusion of semi-symmetric field configurations, which can be thought of as semi-symmetric gravity. The proposed new parameter is relevant not just to the context of (1+3) dimensional gravity but also to the context of semi-symmetric gravity and semi-symmetric field configurations in general. A critical aspect in devising numerical solutions for time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) is preserving inherent properties of the original solution, such as positivity, boundedness, or conservation properties. Although the accuracy of a numerical solution is enhanced when using high-order methods, maintaining these preserving properties often requires sacrificing the order of the method. This issue is addressed in the book chapter presented here, which focuses on implicit time-stepping techniques and explores ways to preserve the underlying properties of a system by employing the Krylov subspace method after applying a transformation to the original system. The chapter begins by examining the maintenance of a particular structure in a simple example, followed by investigating the preservation of a broader class of properties in more complex scenarios. A particular example of a Krylov method is provided, along with a discussion of available implementations. The chapter concludes by reviewing different time-stepping schemes and examining their suitability for preserving certain properties. Although the chapter primarily utilizes the Krylov method with preconditioning, alternatives such as the short-step Peaceman-Rachford scheme are also considered. The chapter aims to offer a balanced view of the topic by incorporating the results of real computations alongside theoretical aspects. Soft-tissue navigation is a complex procedure that requires surgeons to identify and avoid critical structures, particularly in cancer treatments. The process can be made safer with real-time, intraoperative visualization, but achieving this goal poses significant technical challenges. One major obstacle is aligning pre-surgical images with a dynamically changing soft-tissue environment. Our research focuses on developing an automated method for aligning non-rigid tissues using a data-driven finite element model. This model leverages machine learning to accurately depict the distribution and patterns of tissue softness across the surgical site, enabling a 3D registration framework that can keep up with the ever-changing landscape of the soft tissues. Our data-driven approach facilitates real-time prediction of tissue deformation and subsequently, a biomechanical model that can be integrated into 3D registration, resulting in a framework adaptable for various soft tissue modulations, including those encountered during cancer surgeries of the abdomen, thorax, and soft tissues, as well as mastectomies with breast reconstruction. Our research is significant because it paves the way for real-time, intraoperative visualization, bioluminescence imaging, and soft-tissue navigation in various cancer therapies. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for various computer vision tasks, including action prediction and dynamic object segmentation. Although prior research has demonstrated effective use of self-supervised learning for action prediction, its limited application to real-world data has been observed due to the simplistic nature of the training datasets used. In contrast to existing work, this study aims to enhance action prediction models by training them on real-world data involving more complex and heterogeneous motion trajectories. A novel self-supervised learning framework called Adversarial Metric Learning for scene flow is proposed, incorporating an adversarial training mechanism to obtain a general motion trajectory representation that is both compact and diverse. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance in three real-world datasets, including the challenging KITTI dataset, when evaluated using a simple multi-classification model. The beneficial impact of using scene flow data is also quantified by conducting a series of ablation studies. The proposed method has been made publicly available on GitHub. The underlying code is based on the PyTorch deep learning framework and includes both the proposed self-supervised learning training loop and the simple multi-classification model used for evaluation. A ideal matching in a graph is a subset of edges that can be partitioned into disjoint cycles. We establish the relationship between the largest ideal matching and the chromatic index of a cubic graph, ultimately demonstrating that the chromatic index of a cubic graph exceeds its total number of odd cycles by at least 2. Additionally, we discuss how this result can be interpreted in the context of cycle-colourings and Hamiltonian cycles. Moreover, we provide specific examples of graphs that, in addition to containing Hamiltonian cycles, also possess the property of exceeding the total number of odd cycles by at least 4 in their chromatic index. If a cubic graph allows for a 2-factor comprised solely of Hamiltonian cycles, then we prove that its chromatic index exceeds the total number of odd cycles by at least 2, and this result can be further refined to show that the number of edges in each Hamiltonian cycle must be even when considering a decomposition into 2-factors. This paper introduces a new security solution called Timeloops, aimed at preventing malicious data leaks in containerized applications. It achieves this by limiting access to system calls for individual microservices based on a centralized policy framework. However, the key feature of Timeloops is its autonomous capability to create and manage these policies, without requiring manual input. It does this by analyzing the data that each microservice should be operating with, and comparing it to the data each service has access to through the system calls. If a mismatch is detected, the policy is updated accordingly. Moreover, Timeloops is designed to adapt to the evolution of applications over time, without needing manual intervention. It does this by maintaining a historical record of system calls and using it to update the policies accordingly. The results of our evaluation show that Timeloops is not only highly effective in preventing data leaks but also very efficient in terms of computational resources. Furthermore, it detects policy breaches and learns appropriate system call policies for complex applications like Apache Spark and a proxy server combining multiple microservices. The system is also open-source, with the code available on GitHub. The evaluation also included a comparison with another similar solution called OciGate, which is specifically designed to prevent data leaks in Oracle-related applications. The results showed that Timeloops is not only more scalable but also more secure, with a lower false positive rate for data leaks. The validation of Timeloops was carried out using a proxy server with 16 microservices, and the findings were presented at the IEEE Conference on Dependable and Secure Computing (CSDP) in 2021. The learning algorithm for Timeloops now incorporates temporal information, and there is also a feature to ignore system calls that do not affect the data available to the application. After introducing the grid-constrained origin model, the filter implementation, and sensor management strategies, a simulation comparing the proposed filter with a free origin PMBM filter is conducted. Results show that the grid-based approach yields comparable performance with significantly reduced information collection costs. Furthermore, the study demonstrates a path management scenario where the proposed filter excels in reducing data collection costs without compromising accuracy. The proposed filter's grid-based origin model provides a practical and efficient solution for target tracking problems involving large areas of interest. The code for the proposed filter is available online.

The success of a soccer team can be influenced by the critical moments of a game, such as penalties or free kicks. While opponents often employ rigid strategies during these situations, there is room for creative play to gain an advantage. By analyzing European soccer matches, researchers identified a pattern in how teams respond to free kicks in the opponent's territory. They found that instead of aiming for the goal, many teams opt to pass the ball to a specific area, away from the goal, to maintain possession and counter-attack. A deep reinforcement learning approach was used to determine the optimal target areas for these situations, considering various factors like the position of players and game time. It was discovered that choosing the right target area can significantly lower the risk of the opposing team regaining possession and scoring against the attacking team. This knowledge and predictive models can be valuable tools for coaches and teams looking to improve their free kick strategies. A simple and effective action that teams could consider is passing the ball to the spot where the free kick is taken, as this was found to be the most beneficial area in a wide range of scenarios. This research was presented at the IEEE Conference on Computational Intelligence and Games in 2020.

High-frequency seismic data contains valuable information for imaging and reservoir exploration, and a more precise inversion method is needed to process these data effectively. Although least-squares hybrid methods combine the advantages of wave-equation traveltime picking and amplitude-based approaches, they require significant computational resources and cannot handle large-scale, high-frequency data sets in a reasonable timeframe. To make progress in this area, researchers are exploring ways to accelerate these methods, especially by utilizing efficient time-domain extended source signal inversion techniques. Although its application in real-world scenarios is limited due to its rough estimation assumptions, time-domain extended source signal inversion can still be an influential tool, and its integration with hybrid methods could make it even more powerful. If successfully combined, these methods could lead to a significant advancement in seismic data inversion, enabling the precise reconstruction of subsurface structures from high-frequency seismic data. To achieve this, the following steps are proposed: developing scalable time-domain extended source signal inversion code, refining the extraction of extended source signals, and designing a hybrid method that combines time and frequency-domain approaches. If these objectives are met, the resulting framework will be capable of accurately reconstructing subsurface structures from high-frequency seismic data sets. To prevent the unwanted spread of misinformation, it's essential to identify changes that alter the semantic meaning of text. In this work, we focus on detecting semantic alterations that result in text with a different intention or purpose than the original. We analyzed three approaches using contextualized language models: one that uses the distance between original and altered text embeddings, another based on the similarity between their context-dependent representations, and a third utilizing a supervised classification model. Our key observation reveals that contextualized language models can distinguish between semantic and syntactic alterations, as they capture the differences in intention and purpose due to their inherent property of context-dependent representations. Furthermore, we found that the performance of these models relies on the quality of trained parameters rather than input features. We also explored the limitation of using contextualized language models for this task, as they are prone to confusion between semantic alterations that result in a text with a different intention versus those that result in a text with a different purpose. To address this challenge, we propose a simple yet effective strategy called the Intention-Purpose Semantic Alteration Detection Framework, which addresses this issue by incorporating an additional task to train contextualized language models on the differences between purpose and intention contexts. This framework's performance was demonstrated to outperform the baseline approaches in our experiments. We believe this framework has the potential to contribute to the broader task of constructing contextualized language models that capture the nuances of context, as well as the specific challenge of semantic alteration detection. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/semantic-alteration-detection.

This paper explores compressive video recovery and color image demosaicing as two real-world applications for image separation codes. It is now possible to train a single neural network that can recover compressed videos and color images with mosaics simply by training it on a single blurred picture. When applied to compressive video recovery, the model recovers a 64x64 video from a 16x16 blurred picture with a PSNR of 23.6 dB, outperforming a baseline model that recovers 16x16 videos from 16x16 blurred pictures by 0.78 dB. When applied to color image demosaicing, the model recovers a 512x512 color image from a single blurred picture with a PSNR of 23.4 dB, outperforming a baseline model that recovers 512x512 images from 512x512 blurred pictures by 0.5 dB.
