We build a unified framework for cross-lingual semantic mapping and multi-lingual word embedding by leveraging cluster information. A novel cluster-consistent embedding framework is proposed, combining neural network-based embedding with traditional co-occurrence learning, and incorporating a new objective function that ensures the consistency of clusters across languages. Furthermore, a strategy for identifying the optimal set of clusters for multi-lingual embedding is developed. Experiments on multi-lingual embedding demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms rival approaches in tasks like word analogies and semantic similarity computation. Additionally, our method shows that mapping monolingual embeddings across languages using the proposed framework yields superior results in comparison to baseline methods, with a particular improvement in the evaluation of the word-in-word domain. Code for the proposed method is publicly available at: https://github.com/lingua360/CC_WVE.

This study provides first-time data on the fabrication rates of pions, kaons, protons and $\phi$ mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at an energy of 5.44 TeV. Over the course of an study involving 25.92 $\mu$b of integrated luminosity, measured transverse momentum ranges for the aforementioned particles reveal that the fabrication rates of pions, kaons and protons all increase proportionally with transverse energy, while the fabrication rate of $\phi$ mesons exhibits a distinct pattern of increase. Furthermore, the results show that the fabrication rates of the mentioned particles all surpass expected levels based on lead-lead collisions at an energy of 5.52 TeV, with the fabrication rates of pions, kaons and $\phi$ mesons all exceeding such levels by a significant margin. Additionally, studies of particle fabrication in Xe-Xe and lead-lead collisions at the same energy reveal that increasing the size of Xe-Xe collisions to the level of lead-lead collisions results in a significant increase in particle fabrication. Notably, the results agree with calculations based on hydrodynamic models of particle fabrication. A comparative analysis of particle fabrication in Xe-Xe and lead-lead collisions at the same energy also sheds light on the importance of initial state fluctuations in the early stages of heavy ion collisions. In late October 2019, student-led demonstrations erupted in Chile, spreading quickly across the country and becoming the largest protests in its modern history. The rapid dissemination of these protests poses an interesting problem for researchers to explain, given the absence of similar nationwide student movements in recent years. While various factors might contribute to the protests' development, the quick geographic spread suggests that the reactions of people in different locations could be a significant factor. The current study introduces an epidemiological model describing the development and dissemination of the protests on a national level. The proposed model accounts for the protests' spread between nearby and more distant regions and incorporates the effects of decreased connectivity. The study's key finding is that the rapid spread of the protests was likely fueled by strong connections between regions with low and high levels of protest participation, and the protests may have reached a critical point where small increases in protest participation led to a sudden surge across the country. The model's results are supported by real-world data from the 2019 Chilean protests. The proposed model provides a framework for studying the dissemination of other social and cultural phenomena beyond the protests in Chile. Mobile robots and unmanned systems require accurate self-localization ability. Inertial and vision systems provide complementary information, and when combined, can offer a robust and fully autonomous localization method. Previous studies have shown that end-to-end training of visual-inertial state estimation and localization networks can lead to superior performance. This paper presents EMA-VIO, an Enderman-Map-VIO architecture, which utilizes external memory to further enhance performance. Quantum field theory relies on a sophisticated mathematical framework that includes advanced, higher-order differential equations with complex coefficients. Although this sophisticated framework can provide highly accurate results, its intricate nature makes it challenging to integrate into experimental data analysis. A significant improvement in this process is the concept of "semi-quantum" field theory, which uses linear differential equations to analyze certain properties. In this study, we focus on exotic materials known as Weyl semimetals and identify a specific type - those we call "square-root" Weyl materials - whose underlying differential equations can be simplified to a particular form that is essential for validating experimental data and theoretical predictions about these materials. Specifically, this form confirms the unique energy and momentum relationships in these materials and provides a clear explanation for the complex behaviors exhibited by particles and their corresponding antiparticles. This breakthrough also allows us to reintroduce the concept of "semi-quantum" field theory and demonstrate its capabilities on a realistic model of a square-root Weyl material, further enriching our understanding of this rare and fascinating material. This work appears in the journal Physical Review B.

We find this measure to be the absolute difference between the initial and final Bloch vector components. This result can be extended to define a duration-based metric, distinguishing between two types of state changes: those that increase, decrease, or remain constant over time. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between this metric and other asymmetry measures, proposing its use as a lower bound for other, more complex asymmetry measures. This proposed bound is subsequently verified through numerical analysis of random state changes, revealing its effectiveness in capturing the underlying system dynamics. This framework also allows for the derivation of explicit formulas for various asymmetry measures, providing physical interpretations for these measures through example analysis. The result can be generalized to $d$-dimensional systems by examining the behavior of the measure in relation to the system's Hilbert-Schmidt volume. The minimum over time of this volume-based measure reveals its connection to the concept of minimal volume. The connection between the measure and system properties is demonstrated through example analysis of a qutrit system. The proposed framework is further applied to investigate the behavior of the measure in relation to system dynamics, revealing its robustness in capturing the underlying system dynamics. The result is also compared with alternative formulations of the measure, demonstrating its distinction. Given a positively oriented unit vector triangle ABC in the complex plane, this work examines the norm $\|P_{ABC}\|$ of the projection operator $P_{ABC}$ onto the convex region D defined by the triangle's vertices A, B, and C. We derive an inequality for the norm of the difference between the identity operator and the projection operator, initially presented in [3], with a simpler proof. Additionally, we establish the relationship $\|P_{ABC}\|=\sup_{\theta\in[0,\pi/3]}|1-\cos\theta|^{-1}=\sqrt{3}$ and its associated conditions. Further, we explore the behavior of the norm for triangular regions with oblique angles and determine its maximum value of $\sqrt{3}$ when $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy the condition $\alpha+\beta\leq\pi/3$. A lower bound for the norm of the projection operator is also established with the expression $\big(\frac{\alpha\beta}{\sin(\alpha)\sin(\beta)}\big)^{1/2}$, valid for triangular regions defined by the angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and the right angle. A related problem about a square region is then posed. A solution to this problem is provided in the appendix. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying and addressing decoherence in quantum processors. This research highlights the significance of terahertz investigations in evaluating and addressing material flaws in quantum processors. We also explore the terahertz behavior of a coupled-resonator system and discuss its relevance to quantum information processing. This study was conducted at the terahertz scanning near-field optical microscope facility at Kyoto University.

A key aspect of exoplanetary research is understanding how atmospheres of burgeoning planets evolve long-term, especially under varying levels of stellar illumination. This study delves into the long-term atmospheric evolution of terrestrial planets, focusing on the complex balance between internal heat, surface environments, and atmospheric processes that shape their atmospheric chemistry and pressure. A distinguishing feature of our approach is the integration of atmospheric, surface, and mantle processes within a unified framework, allowing for simultaneous analysis of interacting processes that influence each other through various feedback loops. By applying this method to Earth and Mars, we uncovered intricate patterns of process interactions and crucial feedback mechanisms that have significant implications for the atmospheric evolution of these planets. A particular scenario is then simulated, revealing that the current Venus-like atmosphere on Mars was the result of a runaway greenhouse effect caused by increasing solar energy from the young Sun, and that it was followed by a phase of crust cooling that led to volcanic activity and atmospheric processing, ultimately results in the thin atmosphere we observe today. This study also highlights the sensitive dependence of its atmosphere on the internal heat of a planet similar to Venus, and the possible outcome for exoplanets with similar characteristics. This research is relevant to ongoing and future missions such as the PLATO and TLS, which will discover numerous terrestrial exoplanets around the Sun and other similar stars, and to future lander missions that will study the surfaces and atmospheres of these planets in depth. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past events is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model interactions between events of different types. Although nonlinear processes can exhibit complex behavior, including both explosive and fading tendencies, a fundamental question about these processes remains unanswered. In this paper, we develop a Bayesian estimation framework for a specific variant of nonlinear Hawkes processes called the linear-integral Hawkes process. By applying Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, we are able to simulate the underlying components of these processes and thereby gain insights into the behavior of linear-integral Hawkes processes. Our results show that our method can accurately reconstruct the parameters and underlying components of these processes. Additionally, we introduce a new persistence-based statistic called the persistence integral, which provides a comprehensive understanding of these processes. Our findings indicate that the persistence distribution of linear-integral Hawkes processes is concentrated on either the interval [0,1] or [1,∞) and can exchange these intervals behaviorally. Our research also sheds light on the relationship between the persistence distribution and the intensity distribution and reveals that the persistence distribution of linear-integral Hawkes processes exhibits sharp boundaries at $\alpha=1$ or $\beta=1$ when examining the intensity of the process. Our analysis of real data reveals that the persistence integral indicates a state of turbulence in the data corresponding to $t=33$ months and shows that the persistence distribution of the linear-integral Hawkes process exhibits abrupt changes at $t=33$ months. Our research highlights the importance of considering persistence-based metrics for point processes and demonstrates the adaptability of linear-integral Hawkes processes in modeling real data. Our code is available online at https://github.com/abhinavk91/bayesHawkes.

As high-power petawatt laser facilities continue to advance, research is driven by the need to understand and overcome limitations posed by thin targets, including reflection loss, maladaptive polarization behavior, and restricted focusing possibilities. To overcome these constraints and realize full potential, a proposed scheme alters the polarization of intense laser pulses while increasing reflection, with the potential to enhance focusing capabilities and expand target options. This approach leverages a magnetized plasma layer to convert linearly polarized light to circular polarization, with successful experiments demonstrating a 25% boost in reflection and the potential to achieve over 90% reflection in optimized arrangements. This breakthrough offers a versatile tool for (1) waveplate-like purification of irregularly shaped petawatt beams, (2) circular polarization generation for extreme magnetic field creation, (3) improved self-focusing prevention, and (4) access to smaller targets with enhanced symmetry. This novel technique can be applied across a broad spectrum of high-power laser applications. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis reveals that the decoding problem is equivalent to solving a system of linear equations, which can be further transformed into a problem of finding the smallest integer within a specified range that satisfies certain divisibility conditions. This condition can be applied to determine the decodeability of rank metric codes under a specific error level or to determine the largest error size that a code with a given dimension and rank matrix can correct. Additionally, we propose an algorithm for this problem and investigate its computational complexity. For codes with a specific structure, where the rank matrix consists of a single row, we show that there is a simple and efficient way to check decodeability without solving a system of linear equations. This approach is useful for establishing a lower bound on the minimum distance of codes with a single-row rank matrix and shows that there are codes with a single-row rank matrix that exceed the Aardermaij bound. Moreover, we explore the relationship between error correction capability and codebase properties, showing that decodeability is equivalent to the condition that the codebase contains no zero-entry matrix, and we provide a second, stronger condition equivalent to the property that the code has a positive error correction capability. This stronger condition can be checked by examining the rows of the rank matrix, and we demonstrate its implications for the structure of the rank matrix and the existence of codes with specific density characteristics. This includes the result that there are rank metric codes with a single-row rank matrix and any desired density below 49%. Lastly, we investigate the connection between our decodeability condition and the Aardermaij bound, and our results imply that the Aardermaij bound can be tightened, demonstrating this strengthened form of the bound holds true for rank metric codes with a single-row rank matrix. This new form of the bound also yields the result that there are rank metric codes with a single-row rank matrix and any desired density below 49%. This result on density was previously established using an unrelated approach. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson postulated the following combinatorial formula for Pontrjagin classes of differentiable manifolds: the Pontrjagin class of a manifold $M^n$ is the differential form obtained by differentiating the integral of certain polynomial invariants from the tangent space $T_M$. Our research confirms the validity of their predicted formula and provides a mathematical framework to calculate the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold $M^n$ as the differential of a polynomial integral over $T_M$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the classical formula for the Pontrjagin class of a manifold can be obtained by integrating its differential form, thereby establishing a topological counterpart to the proposed equation. The study also examines how the proposed equation can be applied to yield the classical formula for the Euler-Poincaré characteristic, the topological invariant of a manifold. Moreover, we discuss the relationship between the combinatorial and classical formulas for the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold and illustrate the underlying connection using a graphical example. The results presented in this paper were previously published by the authors in a series of articles between 2000 and 2004. The current work is an edited version of those articles. The original source of the combinatorial formula for the Euler-Poincaré characteristic and the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold is attributed to George Maxstew who suggested it in 1991. The proposed formula for the Euler-Poincaré characteristic was validated by Gelfand and MacPherson in 1992, whereas the results related to the Pontrjagin classes were published in 2000. We obtained comprehensive photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo, an supernova that exploded in January 2020, in the nearby galaxy NGC 1431, which is approximately 96 million light years from Earth. Initially, we observed a rise in brightness over two weeks, followed by a short plateau phase of about 30 days, and then the typical decline seen in Type II SNe. The SN entered the nebula phase, shining brightly for an extended period of 130 days. SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent H-alpha line with a double-peaked profile in its early stages, and the expansion velocities of these peaks were distinct, with 13,000 km/s for the higher frequency peak and 6,000 km/s for the lower frequency peak. The electron temperature and abundance of elements like helium, heavy metals, and iron group elements in the SN's gas remained nearly constant. The abundance of elements like oxygen, carbon, and silicon varied significantly, with the highest velocities found for silicon, followed by oxygen and then carbon. The SN's gas expanded at an average velocity of 12,000 km/s and its optical depth was high enough to produce the Balmer lines of hydrogen through recombination, although it wasn't sufficient to absorb most of the ultraviolet light. The presence of the [Fe III] line suggests that the last generated electrons interact with a high degree of ionization, leaving behind mostly iron group elements. The formation of the [Fe III] line also indicates that the SN's gas has a complex structure, with different regions of varying density. The SN's plateau phase lasted for 30 days, which is significantly shorter than the typical 100 days observed in SNe like SN 1970G and SN 1994R. SN~2020jfo's progenitor had a mass between 13 and 15 times that of our Sun, which is similar to the masses found for the progenitors of SNe like SN 1994R and SN 1970G. The analysis of the data suggests that SN~2020jfo exploded due to a massive shock wave caused by core collapse, and that the reduced plateau phase was likely the result of a more massive progenitor. The reduced mass loss also supported this finding, with an estimated mass loss rate between 0.5 and 1 times that of our Sun per year, which is lower than the rates found for SNe like SN 1994R and SN 1970G. To increase the efficiency of wide-field X-ray monitoring with lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a system where multiple LE arrays are aligned at different orientations, allowing for the simultaneous detection of different parts of the X-ray sky. By positioning the LE arrays at 30-degree intervals, we can capture a 4π solid-angle of the sky. Using this setup with 10 LE arrays, each consisting of 1760 pixels, would result in the detection of an event in one pixel across the entire setup with a signal of ~100 counts per second. This system would be suitable for the detection of rare events and could be applied to experiments involving the study of cosmic rays and neutrinos. To reduce the amount of data generated, we suggest a strategy for dividing the LE arrays into smaller regions of interest. The proposed system could also be advantageous for applications in non-X-ray fields such as optical and infrared monitoring. We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a compactness result for sequences of mappings with bounded energy. This approach is applied to prove the smoothness of boundaries of sets arising from monotone operators and variational inequalities, as well as to investigate the behavior of curves influenced by a singular force in the two-dimensional space. Moreover, we introduce a new concept of partial uniform ellipticity for Hamilton-Jacobi equations and demonstrate its relevance in describing the evolution of sets and its impact on the solution's regularity. Finally, we examine the impact of this scenario on the solution's boundary and provide an alternative proof of a result by Swiencki and Székely, initially established for convex functions.

To investigate the connection between dark matter halos and their surrounding cosmic web, researchers have developed methods to identify dark matter halos in simulation data based on velocity information in addition to density. However, the impact of the speed field on halo properties and the mass function of halos is not well understood and requires precise analysis. We employed an artificial neural network to analyze dark matter halos from a large-scale simulation, with the goal of determining how velocity information affects the mass function of halos. By comparing the results to theoretical predictions, we found that the effect of velocity information on the mass function of halos is minimal, but it becomes more significant at high mass scales and may be related to the distribution of velocity field and mass density within the simulation. Additionally, we found that the mass function of halos is essentially the same whether we use velocity information or not, although there are some differences in the high mass end. Furthermore, we analyzed the relationship between the velocity field and mass density within the simulation and found that it can be accurately predicted by a simple power-law model. This model suggests that the cut-off mass density at high masses may vary with the scale over which the velocity field is measured, implying that the mass function of halos has different cut-off values at different scales. This result has important implications for theoretical models of the mass function of halos. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This methodical evolution method starts from an initial, non-equilibrium state and, through the application of a successive over-relaxation algorithm, converges to an equilibrium state. This state is identified by the stability of the solution under the perturbation of a small oscillation. Our methodical evolution method can be repeated for different masses in binary star scenarios to find the corresponding mass transfer boundaries. We have validated our method by successfully replicating the results of previous studies, specifically the finding that low-mass rotating stars in binary systems with low mass ratios undergo Roche lobe instability, and the observation patterns of gamma-ray bursts in high-mass rotating stars in binary systems. Our research has also revealed unique properties of rotating stars in binary systems with mass ratios greater than 1.25, and shows that relativistic rotating stars can exhibit multiple equilibrium configurations, leading to mass transfer boundaries with distinct branches that cannot be predicted by simple stability criteria alone. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

Document extraction models have a cumbersome labeling process that we believe can be significantly simplified. Our innovation involves breaking down the traditional text classification task into two independent tasks: categorizing documents into relevant sections and identifying the data within those sections. This dual-approach reduces labeling costs by focusing on essential document elements rather than entire documents. To achieve this, we introduce a novel technique called Incentivized Data Collection, where workers are paid to label specific document sections instead of entire documents. To encourage the collection of high-quality section labels, we developed a statistical method to predict the accuracy of section labels based on corresponding document labels. This prediction is then used to prioritize the collection of high-confidence section labels. Our experiments on real-world documents demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy and show that quality section labels can be obtained at a significantly lower cost than traditional annotation methods. To further enhance model performance, we propose a simple but effective technique called Section-aware Pretraining. To demonstrate the broader applicability of our approach, we also successfully tested it on other text classification tasks that involve similar annotation costs. Our code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ghru/Document-Extraction- Efficient Annotation. Our approach opens up opportunities to develop more practical and scalable document extraction systems that can be applied across multiple domains. Our findings also highlight the potential of performance-cost tradeoffs in other annotation-intensive text classification tasks. Our future work includes exploring ways to reduce the initial cost of training documents and investigating methods to transfer knowledge from efficiently annotated datasets to new, unlabeled datasets. Our approach has far-reaching implications to make document extraction systems more accessible, affordable, and practical for various real-world applications. Our results suggest that, with some additional setup costs, our efficient annotation method can cut the cost of annotating new documents by as much as 90%. Our approach paves the way for more scalable and self-sustaining document extraction systems that can be developed across multiple domains. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of likely gravitational wave events, posing a significant data processing challenge. To address this issue, we developed an algorithm to swiftly match new gravitational wave events against known neutron star-binary black hole merger signals, which can be scaled up for use on large computing clusters. This method's efficiency in identifying relevant events has been verified through simulated data, and we outline possible extensions to enhance its performance further. Moreover, this research highlights the significance of developing advanced machine learning models capable of distinguishing between different compact binary merger types, and we anticipate our findings will contribute valuable insights to these endeavors. Ultimately, our algorithm is integral to establishing electromagnetic follow-up of compact binary merger candidates and has implications for future gravitational wave observatories, particularly those with simultaneous multi-band observations. During public health crises, people's willingness to engage in urban social interactions may change, potentially leading to varying effects on income diversity of these encounters. While a willingness to socialize more widely might increase the diversity of these interactions, fear of infection could limit such behavior, making diversity less inclusive. Using a longitudinal survey of urban encounters in Tokyo, this study finds that despite a significant decrease in overall social interactions, people's willingness to engage in diverse urban social interactions actually increased. However, this increased desire for diverse interactions did not counter the existing pattern of income segregation observed in pre-pandemic encounters. In fact, it deepened this segregation further, with lower-income individuals experiencing the greatest decline in encounters. This was attributed to reduced access to online platforms facilitating more diverse connections, as well as increased difficulty in encountering strangers in public spaces. The massive protostars, with masses exceeding 30 solar masses, are thought to form through the collapse of massive dense cores. However, the actual origins of these cores are not well understood. I used a numerical model to investigate the development of massive protostars over a decade, with a high-resolution radiative transfer model presenting the results in various wavelengths. The key findings include: the most massive protostars form through the rapid combination of massive star-forming cores, with densities 10^4 times higher than typical prestellar cores; these cores can coalesce either externally, drawn from a massive molecular cloud, or internally, from a self-gravitating disk; once the total mass reached 10 solar masses, the accretion accelerated dramatically, with a rate 10 times greater than earlier phases; the surrounding environments vary greatly, with the most extreme situations seeing the disappearance of a disk in favor of an infalling envelope driven by gravitational force; the eventual death of these massive protars will result in the formation of either massive white dwarfs or neutron stars, with the surrounding matter forming a dense, rotating core. The outcomes depend heavily on the specific accretion history. The most common situations will result in the formation of 3-4 solar mass white dwarfs, with the remaining matter in the form of a rotating, dense core equivalent to about 1-2 solar masses. The most extreme situations, with the formation of extremely dense rotating cores equivalent to Chandrasekhar limits, are less common. The possible detection of these extremely dense cores, with the characteristics similar to those of pulsar parents, could provide valuable insights into the formation mechanisms of massive star-forming regions. The model is consistent with observations, but also predicts the existence of extremely dense rotating cores, which could be detected through the identification of pulsar parents born from massive protostars. The possible locations of these objects could be found in the molecular clouds W51, OMC 1, and G333.758-0.744, with the specific identification of dense rotating cores requiring more sensitive observations in the form of pulsar surveys. The formation of massive star-forming regions remains poorly understood, with the current models relying on random collapses of dense cores. This research investigates how a uniform current affects shallow water gravity waves in an infinite, two-dimensional still water of finite depth. A new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation is derived to model this scenario, and through numerical analysis, we examine the effects of a uniform current on wave energy, circulation, and the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation's validity. Our results show that the new Dysthe equation accurately captures the transformation of waves in the presence of a uniform current, and we propose a modification to the existing Dysthe equation including circulation to extend its applicability to this particular case. Furthermore, we find that the new Dysthe equation can be related to the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and this connection is explored in the paper. Additionally, we examine the new Dysthe equation's behavior in the laboratory setting and find that it can be applied to waves with amplitudes up to 15% and a uniform current with a strength up to 3 times the wave speed. The paper is concluded by discussing the new Dysthe equation's potential applications, along with its limitations and possible future improvements. The associated computer code is made publicly available for further development and use. The new Dysthe equation provides a valuable tool for predicting the evolution of long surface waves in the presence of a uniform current in the laboratory setting. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our analysis identifies key patterns of high-frequency fake news articles, demonstrating the diversity of this category of information. The code for this project is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/abhishek2911/Fake-News-Summarization. Moreover, a live demo is available at https://fake-news-summarization.herokuapp.com/.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as gold standards for training and testing NLP models. However, annotated data also incur significant costs, particularly in regards to large-scale projects. A potential advancement in NLP workflows could be the incorporation of semi-supervised learning techniques. In this process, models are trained on top of existing annotated data, and then used to facilitate high-efficiency human annotation. Specifically, we propose a novel method called EasyFix, which leverages a BERT-based model to produce partially annotated data samples. These partial annotations are subsequently reviewed by human annotators, with only a single word being added to each data sample. Our experiments Leverage a dataset called EMEB, which comprises emotion-related binary questions annotated with three semantic categories. The results show that the EasyFix framework yields accurate annotations, with a particular advantage in regards to the annotation of rare semantic categories. Moreover, we discover that a single round of annotation based on the EasyFix framework is sufficient to obtain high performance on the EMEB dataset when used for classification tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ASU-NLP-Seoul/EasyFix.

In object-based programming for GPUs, memory allocation and access are both critical and challenging tasks. Although current approaches, such as using fixed-size arrays or global memory, facilitate rapid development, they lead to inefficient memory usage, suboptimal performance, and increased safety risks. Conversely, manual memory management via low-level functions in languages like CUDA and OpenCL offers superior performance and low overhead, but demands advanced expertise and significant performance benefits come at the expense of dramatically increased programming complexity. Between these extremes, there is a notable gap in the market for easy-to-use, high-performance memory management, particularly for large-scale applications. To address this issue, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed to streamline object allocation and management on GPUs. This allocator employs a segment-based approach, dividing memory into fixed-sized blocks that can be allocated and managed efficiently. A novel, multi-threaded garbage collection mechanism is also introduced to reclaim memory from unused objects, further enhancing performance and memory utilization. Developed using CUDA, DynaSOAr includes a type system and memory access optimizations to ensure both safety and high throughput. Our evaluation shows that DynaSOAr offers substantial performance improvements and better memory efficiency in various object-based applications for GPUs. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's API is compatible with OpenCL, enabling the use of this allocator in OpenCL programs as well. To facilitate OpenCL integration, we developed a command-line tool that converts CUDA binaries to OpenCL binaries. DynaSOAr is an open-source project available on GitHub. To facilitate replication and further development, our evaluation code and benchmark datasets are also publicly accessible. With its ease of use, high performance, and efficient memory management, DynaSOAr provides a reliable foundation for building complex, object-based GPU applications in various fields, including scientific simulations, data analytics, and artificial intelligence. Our analysis indicates that this allocator offers a suitable answer to the significant challenge of managing memory in large-scale GPU applications with multiple threads. To take advantage of DynaSOAr's features in OpenCL development, it is necessary to learn the CUDA version of the compiler. Although DynaSOAr provides a command-line tool for converting CUDA binaries to OpenCL binaries, this conversion process is inefficient and may not support all OpenCL platforms. Consequently, this may pose some difficulties for developers already familiar with OpenCL but not CUDA. We investigated the electronic and magnetic framework of carbon and nitrogen defects within the rutile TiO2 structure. Our calculations showed that both elements can form stable bonds with titanium, but nitrogen has a greater affinity due to its smaller size, allowing it to form a magnetic moment at the N-Ti-N site. With increased doping levels, the magnetic moments at the N sites merge to form a spin density along the c-axis of the crystal structure. Conversely, carbon dotted regions do not exhibit magnetism. The presence of both nitrogen and carbon defects can lead to visible absorption in the range of 3-5 eV and influence the band gap of TiO2. Notably, nitrogen defects can create energy levels within the band gap of TiO2. Our research suggests that both N and C doped TiO2 could have useful applications, including the reduction of reflectivity and enhancement of photocatalytic properties. Additionally, we found that boron, as a p-element, may also be suitable for doping TiO2, with predicted stable bond formations and potential for energy levels within the band gap.

This is known as Erdos-Katona conjecture. Another notable problem in Ramsey theory is the rich graph problem, initially posed by Erdos, Stone, and Turan in 1938. It asks for the smallest number $r(n)$ such that every edge coloring of a complete graph of order $n$ contains a monochromatic subgraph with at least one free vertex. In this paper, we explore an intermediate concept called upper richness, and prove that every edge coloring of a complete graph of order $n$ contains a subgraph of size at least $r(n)$ with the property that the largest subgraph with one free vertex is bipartite. Additionally, we establish a lower bound for the smallest number $r(n)$ such that every edge coloring of a complete graph of order $n$ contains a monochromatic subgraph with at least one free vertex, and determine specific values for $r(5)$ and $r(6)$. Moreover, we offer an inductive framework to extend our approach to larger values of $n$. Lastly, we examine the relationship between these problems and provide an alternate proof of a recent result regarding the Erdos-Katona conjecture. Finally, we establish an alternative characterization of minimal simple groups equivalent to a result by M. Aschbacher. This research paper is concluded by exploring the potential expansion of its main theorem to include a broader class of groups. The flow behavior of liquid foams is significantly influenced by the texture of their surface.  A recent study revealed the existence of a particular cell wall regime, characterized by a sudden and marked increase in friction.  This phenomenon was found to result from the unique interaction between the vertical cell walls and the moving surface, creating an asymmetrical pattern as the surface flows to the sides.  This pattern consists of channels and sinuses, and its stability is critical in understanding the abrupt increase in friction.  A computational analysis showed that the emergence of this pattern can be attributed to the sudden appearance of a sticky state in the cell wall texture.  This sticky state is induced by the sudden increase in the radius of curvature of the cell walls and results in a sharp and significant escalation in frictional forces.  The resulting cell wall texture also exhibits a complex dynamics, with channels and sinuses continuously merging and splitting.  This complex behavior is stable and has been observed in repeated experiments, demonstrating the robustness of this texture-induced regime.  It also gives rise to a distinctive sound emission, likely a hallmark of this regime.  A computational analysis of the cell wall texture allows for the extraction of relevant information, enabling the prediction of the onset of the sticky state, the cell size distribution, and the sound emission phenomenon.  This knowledge provides a deeper understanding of the intricate dynamics of liquid foams and offers a novel approach to controllably varying their texture-induced behavior.  The possibility of transferring this knowledge to other complex systems with similar cell-like structures is also discussed.  The possible connections to other phenomena, such as granular gases, dry friction, and nonlinear oscillations, are explored in the companion paper by van Hoogman et al. titled: Nonlinear Dynamics of a Liquid Foam Surface.  The study was published in the journal Physical Review Letters vol. 125, no. 12 (2020).

In neural machine translation, the focus is typically set to translate one phrase at a time, with attention weights determined locally by source and target context. However, this restrictive approach may not work optimally in certain situations, such as when translating long sentences that span different topics. To explore this limitation, we investigate an optimal focus policy using deep reinforcement learning, and find that a look-ahead focus strategy of up to three phrases outperforms the traditional local focus policy by a 3% absolute improvement in BLEU score, with significant gains in specific challenging cases. To further analyze this phenomenon, we examine the distribution of optimal focus weights and observe that the preferred policy often coincides with structural marks of the input sentence. To incorporate this preferred policy into standard attention networks would require additional learnable parameters, but we show that simple look-ahead focus policies can be used as a substitute, with comparable performance gains. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-MLG-NLP/NMTRF.

Our investigation provides a detailed analysis of the impact of the J/ψ decay into a photon and missing momentum on two effective field theories: one for neutrino and one for dark matter. By comparing the cross-section for the process γ + J/ψ, we determine the corresponding limits on neutrino and dark matter four-fermion interactions. Specifically, we derive constraints on the energy scale Λν/R and ΛDM/R in the relevant effective field theories. Furthermore, we establish a connection between these two energy scales, demonstrating their proportionality to the square of the J/ψ mass. Alongside this discovery, we examine the contribution of the J/ψ γ decay to the total annihilation cross-section for neutros, providing a quantitative assessment for both νν and ν¯ν systems. Additionally, we explore the implications of these findings for the energy at which four-fermion interactions become important in QCD, and reveal that this energy lies above 10 GeV for both neutrino and dark matter systems. Consequently, we expect the study of initial-state radiation in proton-proton collisions to be relevant for investigating these interactions at higher energies. Given the limited data available for the J/ψ γ decay width, we acknowledge that our analysis incorporates an estimate based on a related process, namely the ϒ γ decay width. Consequently, any future determination of this width will enable a more precise investigation of the underlying physics. Lastly, we propose that experiments collecting large samples of J/ψ particles, particularly those operating at or beyond the top energy of 5.9 GeV, can engage in deep searches for four-fermion interactions in both neutrino and dark matter systems.

This convergence holds for any initial condition and is independent of the walk's initial state. This result can be interpreted as the convergence of the walk's occupation time at the origin to a specific distribution in the metric $d_T$, given that the walk's initial state is equal to the mean, which is far from the origin. This finding is a specific case of a more general theorem that states that the scaled local time at any point $x$ also converges to a non-degenerate distribution in the metric $d_T$. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and a 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of plasma wave propagation. This mode is critical for converting most of the power from the waves to heat in the plasma, rather than losing it to electron trapping. To confirm the plasma source was operating in the helicon mode, a study was conducted of how plasma parameters such as density and electric field varied along the length of the plasma source, comparing the results with existing helicon mode plasma models. The study found that the plasma source effectively maintained a constant electric field along its length, and offered a range of density profiles by adjusting the magnetic field, all while operating efficiently with low power consumption. It was also discovered that a specific configuration, with a dense plasma region near the end of the source and a gradual density transition towards the antenna, could be achieved by increasing the magnetic field beyond a certain point, and that this mode was insensitive to misalignments of the antenna and was therefore a stable configuration for plasma sources. The results of the study are relevant to the design of future plasma sources for ICRF applications. The validation of the helicon mode and the characterization of the plasma source will contribute to the improvement of existing models, and provide a tool for predicting plasma parameters in similar sources. The validated parameters of the IShTAR plasma source are now part of international databases, and the experience gained will benefit the design of future sources, such as the STEP plasma source. The findings of this study have been compared to results obtained from a larger version of the IShTAR plasma source, which features a 1 meter length and a 0.5 meter diameter, and show that increasing the size of the source leads to a transition away from the helicon mode, and results in a less efficient mode of plasma wave propagation called the mode mixing regime. The experience gained from this study will be applied to the design of future sources, such as the STEP plasma source. The results of this study have been published in the journal Plasma Sources Science and Technology. The authors of the study are M. Anton, J. B. Stratton, G. Ray, R. McLean, G. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), have gained significant practical value in processing complex and irregular data patterns. Despite their practical applications and outstanding performance, the underlying principles of GCNs, particularly for data representing non-euclidean spaces, lack a clear intuitive interpretation. In contrast to traditional frequency-domain analyses of conventional CNNs that reveal important insights into their functionality, a similar exploration of GCNs within the frequency domain is hindered by the absence of a well-established theoretical framework for Fourier transforms on graph theory. As a result, the fundamental working mechanism of GCNs appears mysterious. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by introducing a frequency-domain analysis of GCNs, offering a concise and self-contained introduction to Fourier transforms on graphs. We then outline three key aspects - spatial signal variation, data formatting issues, and feature transformation - that together comprise the underlying functioning mechanism of GCNs. We hope this research will be beneficial to both seasoned academics and practicing engineers seeking to deepen their understanding of GCNs. Moreover, this study's approach can be reinterpreted as a form of'matched filtering' that unlocks new design possibilities for GCNs, particularly in tasks involving audio or graphical signal processing. All necessary mathematical proofs and exploratory research can be accessed in the supplementary materials section. For the sake of clarity and convenience, this study assumes readers have a basic understanding of conventional CNNs and basic graph theory, but comprehensive overviews of these topics are also provided in the appendix. For those interested in implementing the frequency-domain analysis of GCNs, a sample code is available online. This study's findings and suggestions are further validated through a series of experimental trials conducted on well-known GCN datasets. These experiments demonstrate the value of the frequency-domain analysis approach and provide a foundation for future research and possible applications. They also highlight the complex nature of GCN learning and signal noise, and propose three possible future research directions. This study and its findings are expected to benefit a range of fields, including biology, medicine, remote sensing, and finance, among others. It is also hoped that this work will spark a broader theoretical investigation into the frequency-domain properties of GCNs. This research was conducted without the support of any external funding. All necessary permissions for the reuse of listed datasets can be found in the text referring to their original sources. The authors wish to acknowledge the contributions of multiple anonymous reviewers whose feedback was invaluable in refining this study. They also express their gratitude to the original creators of the PyTorch and PyG deep learning frameworks used in this research

This leads to significant reductions in dimensionality, facilitating convenient and efficient data processing, analysis, and visualization. Our research focuses on developing a computationally efficient and statistically robust algorithm to automate the process of selecting these center points, with a specific goal of identifying a small number of points that minimize the maximum distance between any data point and its nearest center. We have designed a primal-dual algorithm to solve this problem, which results in a cluster structure that not only accurately represents the data but also has a mathematically provable guarantee of data coverage. Furthermore, our solution has a guaranteed performance compared to an optimal solution obtained through a more complex dynamic programming approach. We introduce a novel framework for strategic reasoning in uncertain environments, labeled as Hierarchical Decompositions of POMDPs (HDPs). This framework converges to an optimal strategy for a significant class of POMDPs, specifically those where future states can be influenced by previous actions within a limited horizon. We show that HDPs with a first-layer POMDP are solved when the second-layer POMDPs reduce to single-state POMDPs. We further establish that stationary policies are sufficient for an important subclass of POMDPs known as hidden-state POMDPs. This is illustrated by a hidden-state POMDP representation of a famous chase-evasion problem, the "Lion and the Grid", where hierarchical decompositions yield a significant reduction in the size of the problem compared to traditional POMDP representations. This serves as an instance where future states are independent of current actions beyond a fixed horizon and hierarchical decompositions provide a precise characterization of this property. This framework and its benefits are also demonstrated through an analysis of hierarchical decompositions for the "Lion and the Grid" problem, showing that future states can be influenced by previous actions within a limited horizon. This cannot be captured by future-state independence properties derived from hierarchical decompositions. This research is significant because it contributes a new and general framework for strategic reasoning in uncertain environments, provides a precise characterization of future-state independence properties, offers a compact and efficient representation of POMDPs, and offers an analysis of its own benefits and limitations. This could potentially be applied to a wide range of complex POMDP domains, including many real-world domains. This is further demonstrated by showing that hidden-state POMDPs are solvable in polynomial time, providing an efficient solution to the well-known lion and grid problem, and other similar chase-evasion problems. This is in contrast to previous results which showed a separation between hidden-state POMDPs and POMDPs to be undecidable, but this was for general POMDPs and not for the specific class of hidden-state POMDPs. This is in fact a result that holds for the specific class of hidden-state POMDPs, but not for the more general category of POMDPs. In multi-task reinforcement learning, agents typically face the problem of their performance suffering on non-current tasks due to an excessive focus on recent experiences. This issue is particularly pronounced in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning, where the difficulty is compounded by the challenge of balancing exploration and leveraging knowledge from prior experiences. Our proposed method, called Separation Module Learning, targets this problem by dividing tasks into distinct spheres of influence, where tasks within the same domain share a common state representation. This approach enables the agent to develop a state distribution that is unique to each task domain, thereby preventing performance degradation on non-current tasks. In our experiments, this approach was shown to excel in both simple and complex scenarios, with performance gains observed in tasks that require a high level of expertise. Our code is available online at github.com/xxx/SMLTNet. Moreover, we present a theoretical analysis of the relationship between the size of a task domain and the difficulty of learning a single state representation that encompasses all tasks within that domain. This theoretical aspect was previously unexplored in the field of multi-task reinforcement learning. Our findings suggest that the number of states that can be represented within a single state space is directly proportional to the number of visits required to explore a given task domain fully. This is a significant discovery because it highlights the problem of experiencing a sudden drop in performance on a previously learned task due to a change in the environment that requires additional exploration in that task domain. Our results also demonstrate the practical advantages of this approach in real-world applications, with performance gains observed in both small and large-scale scenarios, including complex scenarios with multiple sub-domains. This is a significant achievement because it breaks the previous barrier in the field of multi-task reinforcement learning, where the number of tasks that can be learned simultaneously was limited to a few dozen. In our current record, we successfully trained a model on 100 tasks that are distributed across 10 distinct sub-domains, with each sub-domain containing anywhere from 5 to 20 tasks that require a different state representation. This achievement opens up new possibilities for this approach in real-world applications, where there are numerous tasks that need to be learned simultaneously, with performance that is comparable to the results achieved in simpler scenarios. Our findings suggest that the proposed method of Separation Module Learning is particularly well-suited for solving problems in areas like multi-agent reinforcement learning, with multiple agents that need to cooperate with each other, as well as areas that involve learning multiple complex skills that are distinct from each other. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on capturing the posterior distribution of all possible restorations. The interstellar medium is home to numerous regions with varying properties, and mapping these regions is a major goal for astronomical research. Pulsar scintillometry can analyze the interstellar medium and identify these regions, even when observing a single source. By applying this method to data from the VRO P3XV 0.77-4.75 GHz radio observatory, researchers have discovered new regions in the line of sight to the pulsar B1133+16. These findings suggest that this particular line of sight contains a significant amount of gas with high temperatures and a high level of turbulence, as well as a large solid angle of anomalous scintillation, likely caused by a nearby star-forming region. Additionally, they have identified two distinct regions in the line of sight, each with its own distinct characteristic scintillation pattern. This success paves the way for similar investigations of other pulsars, and highlights the potential of combined efforts between observational groups and model developers to uncover the detailed structure of the interstellar medium. This research was conducted as part of the PULSAR MULTIBAND EXPERIMENT (PULME) project.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through a pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural network. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation by utilizing convolutional layers with causal connections to model long-term dependencies in audio waveforms. However, the restricted pitch control of WN is attributed to its fixed dilation convolutional layers, which results in the network being unable to effectively capture periodic signals at unknown frequencies, particularly evident in polyphonic sound generation. To overcome this limitation, QPNet introduces a dynamic dilation convolutional network, where each layer possesses a distinct frequency support to adaptively capture signals with varying periods, informed by a probability distribution estimated from input data. The experimental results on both single- and multi-speech data sets demonstrate the improved pitch control of QPNet in comparison to WN and a currently prevalent model, also showing its enhanced sample efficiency in unconditional audio generation. Moreover, QPNet surpasses the state-of-the-art models in conditional single-speech generation and exhibits a notable improvement in multi-speech generation, particularly in polyphonic scenarios, as it can generate sounds with deeper period structures and more diverse signal combinations. The code for QPNet is publicly available at: https://github.com/Shoukai-Huang/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

Deep neural networks like ResNets have demonstrated superior performance in various image classification tasks. However, these networks fail at localizing visual noises when trained to classify images. Researchers have proven that deep neural networks are inherently prone to noise robustness when trained to minimize the l2 norm of the output. Yet, the same level of robustness isn't extended to the l1 norm, enabling the creation of adversarial attacks that mislead the networks. To complicate things further, noise robustness under the l1 norm isn't necessarily a hallmark of noise robustness under the l0 norm, which represents the number of pixels that are altered in an image. Intuitively, one might assume that networks trained for robustness against noises that alter a single pixel would be resistant to certain visual patterns like the number 7. But our experiments surprisingly show that such assumptions are incorrect and demonstrate a challenging task called visual noise localization, which involves identifying the pixels altered by a noise that appears in an image. By analyzing the findings, we reveal that the challenge lies in distinguishing between noises that affect the low-frequency and high-frequency image features, demonstrating that the task can be simplified by demonstrating that networks trained for robustness against noises that alter the high-frequency features of an image aren't resistant to patterns like the number 7, which primarily reside in the low-frequency domain. This discovery is further solidified by creating a robust adversarial noise that alters the high-frequency features of an image without compromising the task's primary goal of image classification. To overcome this challenge, we propose a new task called visual noise localization and explore the underlying mechanics through the use of a simple and effective approach that involves adding a new regression head to the network, demonstrating that the networks are capable of learning the noise's silhouette even when the noise occupies a small portion of the image. The proposed approach is then utilized to investigate the fundamental challenge that resides in the network's noise robustness under the l0 norm, providing actionable insights that could be valuable for future research. The code for this work is publicly available at github.com/vladimir157/dnlf. The proposed approach has been tested and validated through a series of rigorous experiments, demonstrating its capabilities and the complexity of the noise robustness under the l0 norm. The results are significant because they provide novel insights into the noise robustness of deep neural networks and could pave the way for future breakthroughs in areas like the discovery of simple visual elements and patterns in images. To evaluate the effects of this image editing on reports, we compare them to corresponding original reports using a novel metric called the "edit distance per location," which breaks down the differences between reports on a feature-by-feature basis. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates the exploration of complex data sets. The application
is user-friendly, with a simple and intuitive graphical interface, and offers
options for exporting visualizations to external applications, taking screenshots
of the 3D scenes, and generating reports on the data analysis. ViDaExpert is
particularly well-suited for biotechnology research, molecular biology, and
genomics, and supports a wide range of file formats commonly used in these fields.
